headline: US Treasury Traders Make Bullish Bets Ahead of Jobs Report
author: Victor Swezey

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Bond traders are positioned for further gains for the Treasury market ahead of Friday's October employment report as expectations for additional Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes continue to fade.

A global stock selloff in the wake of US midterm elections has driven investors to the safety of US bonds this week, taking yields to the lowest levels since early September on Thursday. The 10-year rate was at 4.82% on Friday as the equity rout worsened.

The recent gains emboldened traders to target even lower yields in the coming days. In the options market, one trade anticipated the 10-year yield could reach 4.7% by the end of next week, while another, expiring on Nov. 20, targeted a decline to around 4.35%.

While expected to show improvement from September, the October jobs data — even if stronger than anticipated — could still see the Treasury rally continue to the extent that investors are poised to buy a selloff.
"We'd be more likely to buy more than we would to sell" if there's a firm print, said Jamie Patton, co-head of global rates at the TCW Group.

Patton's view jibes with the finding of a survey by strategists at BMO Capital Markets Inc. Though "cautiously biased toward higher yields," investors are "looking to add duration on a post-payrolls selloff in Treasuries," strategists led by Vail Hartman said in a report. BMO's monthly survey of how investors intend to react to a shift in Treasury yields sparked by the jobs data found that 48% would buy a dip in prices, compared with a six-month average of 43% and the most in four months.

The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023 after an oil price surge caused by the US war on Iran kept inflation elevated, while the AI investment boom buoyed US stocks. Since then, however, expectations for further hikes have been eroded, particularly after the central bank stood pat in October, saying economic conditions permitted waiting for additional data to guide its next decision on Dec. 9.

Interest-rate swaps are pricing in a roughly 68% chance of a December rate increase and less than fully pricing in two quarter-point hikes by mid-2027. As recently as last month, the contracts fully priced in three hikes by that point.

"We're expecting somewhat softer data on Friday, but for markets it's still very much about the fundamentals," said Gennadiy Goldberg, head of US interest rates strategy at TD Securities. "We're still looking at an economy that's pretty strong and a labor market that's 'low-hire, low-fire,' so we've priced out a lot of rate hikes over the course of the last couple of weeks."

By the time Fed policymakers meet in December, they'll have seen November employment data as well, slated to be released Dec. 4. They'll also have in hand inflation indicators to be released later this month — the October consumer price index on Nov. 10, and the personal consumption expenditures (or PCE) price gauges in October personal income and spending data on Nov. 25.

This week's slump in crude oil prices to the lowest levels in two months — driven in part by the prospect that the election results will bring about a swifter end to the Iran war — has spurred a collapse in market-implied inflation expectations. The breakeven rate for five-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS — representing the average CPI rate needed to match the return from higher-yielding regular Treasuries — declined to about 2.27% this week from 2.5% at the end of last week.

The October jobs report, to be released Friday at 8:30 a.m. in Washington, is expected to show nonfarm payrolls increased by 65,000, the median estimate in a Bloomberg survey. September's 29,000 increase was weaker than every estimate in the survey, but faces revision in the October report.

"The last two or three months, it seems like we get a huge revision one way and then next month it's revised back," said Oliver Chambers, head of fixed income SMA at Clark Capital Management. "That slowdown has to normalize a little bit."
